overview: Abenaki history belongs to the forests and waterways of Ndakina, an ancestral homeland spanning southern Québec and parts of the northeastern United States. The W8banaki Nation continues through Odanak, Wôlinak and members living elsewhere. Its history includes seasonal food gathering, skilled making, diplomacy and continuing institutions for knowledge and community life.

periods.title: The fortified village at Odanak
periods.summary: Around 1704, Abenaki residents and French allies built a fortified village beside the Saint-François River. Its archaeological remains illuminate a particular community within the wider Abenaki world.

periods.title: An attack on Odanak
periods.summary: In October 1759, Robert Rogers’s British force attacked Odanak, killing inhabitants and burning its buildings. Contemporary accounts disagree sharply about the number killed.

periods.title: Basket making supports households
periods.summary: From about 1870, basket making became a major source of income at Odanak and Wôlinak. Family businesses connected inherited craft skills with markets beyond their communities.

periods.title: A community museum
periods.summary: The Musée des Abénakis began in 1965, creating a lasting place at Odanak for sharing history and cultural knowledge.

periods.title: Cooperation between communities
periods.summary: The organisation now called W8banaki was founded in 1979 as a tribal council joining Odanak and Wôlinak. It supports representation, development and administration for its member communities.

items.text: The Nation’s history describes spring and summer gatherings beside lakes and rivers, followed by smaller family hunting groups in the interior during colder seasons. Canoes and portages linked fishing places, hunting territories and settlements.

Food came from hunting, fishing, gathered plants and, in suitable areas, maize, beans and squash. Gardening varied with climate and locality; it supplemented other food work rather than making every community follow an identical farming calendar.

sections.title: What the ground at Odanak reveals

items.text: In 2012, archaeologist Geneviève Treyvaud described postholes thought to lie near the fort’s palisade. These were traces used to reconstruct a vanished structure, rather than a complete defensive wall surviving above ground.

The excavation found hearths used for copperworking, kettle fragments and small metal cones. Makers cut imported kettles into pieces and reshaped the copper into tinkling ornaments for clothing or hair, adapting traded material to local purposes.
A French liard minted in 1657 was also recovered. That date belongs to the coin; it does not establish the fort’s construction year or the beginning of Abenaki occupation.

Odanak and Wôlinak basket makers wove black ash splints with sweetgrass. Families made baskets during winter and travelled to Ontario and the United States in summer to sell them. Some businesses employed additional Abenaki and French-Canadian workers.

Basket sales became especially important as settlement and timber extraction restricted access to hunting grounds. In the early twentieth century, customs duties, dearer sweetgrass, competition and wartime loss of demand reduced profits. Craft knowledge nevertheless continued to be taught.

Young Abenaki apprentices participated in the Fort Odanak excavations alongside archaeologists. A 2017 museum publication brought the project’s results to a wider public, connecting archaeological research with the community whose past was being studied.

Gordon M. Day’s Western Abenaki Dictionary, published in 1994, records language spoken in the later twentieth century. Written for readers beyond specialist linguists, it offers a resource for learners as well as a record of spoken knowledge.

Abenaki language teaching at the Université de Sherbrooke links pronunciation and conversation with oral tradition. Lessons address family, food, animals, weather and place names, showing how language learning can connect directly with daily life.

Abenaki filmmaker Alanis Obomsawin came to cinema through performance and storytelling and joined the National Film Board as a consultant in 1967. Her work made documentary film a medium for Indigenous histories and voices.

Her 1993 film Kanehsatake: 270 Years of Resistance documents the 1990 confrontation over Kanien’kéhaka lands at Oka. The filmmaker is Abenaki; the community at the centre of this film is Kanien’kéhaka, or Mohawk.

The Ndakina Office combines historical, archaeological and environmental research with community knowledge. Its Guardians initiative, active since 2021, supports care for habitats and food sources and education about the ancestral territory.

ending.text: Colonial expansion restricted land access and transformed Abenaki livelihoods. The people continued, maintaining and renewing basket making and other knowledge. Odanak and Wôlinak remain living communities with their own councils, cooperating through W8banaki; the loss of a fort or a hunting territory was not the end of Abenaki history.

sources.title: W8banaki, Histoire de la Nation
sources.note: Community history, sections on the Nation, seasonal subsistence and colonial pressures; no ancient archaeological site is equated with a modern political founding.

sources.title: Musée des Abénakis, An Archaeological Project and a Fort
sources.note: Excavation account and published interview transcript: postholes, copperworking and a dated coin. Findings are distinguished from interpretations.

sources.title: Musée des Abénakis, The River Burns
sources.note: Same virtual exhibition as the excavation account; combined paraphrase budget. Conflicting casualty totals are not resolved into a single number.

sources.title: Parks Canada, Abenaki Basket-Making Industry, 1870 to 1920
sources.note: Materials, family production, seasonal sales and economic pressures; 1870 is an industry phase, not the invention of basketry.

sources.title: Musée des Abénakis, institutional history and activities
sources.note: Museum established in 1965, educational activities and exhibitions; no claim that culture began with the museum.

sources.title: Musée des Abénakis, The Abenakis of Odanak: an archaeological journey, 2017
sources.note: Publication announcement and community participation in excavations. The announcement was read, not the complete book.

sources.title: W8banaki, Notre mission
sources.note: Formation in 1979, Odanak and Wôlinak membership and institutional mission.

sources.title: W8banaki, Ndakina Office
sources.note: Community research, environmental work and the Guardians initiative beginning in 2021.
